subject: The World Around Us
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 13 periods = 520 minutes
Total: 13 periods · 8h 40min

periods.textbook_anchor: How is Waste Created? — Discuss the picture of children and a teacher cleaning a park (p. 150)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 150 illustration of park-cleaning scene

time_bands.activity: Teacher displays Textbook p. 150 and asks children to look quietly at the picture before anyone speaks. Children point out what they notice — who is in the scene, what objects appear, what the people seem to be doing.

Whole-class discussion: Why are the children and teacher cleaning the park? Have you ever seen piles of waste near your home or school? How do you think that waste got there? Children share freely; teacher captures key ideas on the board without judging any response.

Children recall everyday activities — cooking, eating, shopping, playing, school work — and think about what waste each activity leaves behind. In pairs they talk through one activity each, then share with the class. Teacher builds a growing class list on the board: peels, wrappers, paper scraps, tins, old clothes, pencil shavings.

Whole group reflects: of all the waste types on the board, which surprised you most? Children choose one type and say one sentence about where it comes from. Teacher closes by affirming that noticing waste is the first step to managing it well.

periods.implied_lo: Students can identify everyday human activities as sources of different types of waste.
periods.section_context: Park-cleaning picture, old clothes, tins, bottles, paper, vegetable and fruit peels, plastic wrappers, pencil shavings, old batteries.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask children to think about what their family did between waking up and coming to school — what scraps or wrappers were left behind? This near-to-self prompt surfaces a wide variety of waste types without prompting.

periods.textbook_anchor: How is Waste Created? — Recall different activities done during the day, identify the waste created, and share findings with classmates (p. 150)

time_bands.activity: Teacher recaps the class list of waste types built previously (from memory, retelling the ideas — not a named earlier unit). Children close their eyes and picture their morning at home. What did they use? What was thrown away?

Children open notebooks and draw a simple two-column table: Activity | Waste it creates. They fill in as many rows as they can independently, thinking about the whole day — morning routine, meals, schoolwork, play. Teacher circulates and prompts quietly.

Children share their tables in groups of four, listening for activities and waste types they had not thought of. Groups then choose their most surprising activity-waste pair to share with the class. Teacher notes these on the board, highlighting variety.

Quick whole-class reflection: Is there any activity in our day that creates no waste at all? Children discuss briefly, noticing that waste is produced by almost everything. Teacher affirms the observation without prescribing a conclusion.

periods.implied_lo: Students can record and share observed connections between daily activities and the waste those activities produce.
periods.section_context: Daily activities (cooking, eating, shopping, school tasks, play), waste types produced (peels, wrappers, paper, tins, old items).
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: If children mention their elders' activities — cooking, sewing, fixing things — welcome those; they often surface a richer range of waste types and naturally invite reflection on traditional versus modern habits.

periods.activity_title: Waste and Its Harm — Observing Our School Surroundings
periods.textbook_anchor: Ways to Manage Waste — Observe the surroundings of the school (p. 152)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 152 content on harms of unmanaged waste

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads aloud the harms described on Textbook p. 152 — animals dying from eating plastic, harmful gases from burning plastic, mosquitoes breeding in stagnant wastewater — pausing after each for children to react. Children share if they have seen or heard of any of these situations.

Children stand up and walk slowly around the classroom and, if safe, glance into the corridor or school ground. They observe quietly: Is there any waste lying around? Where exactly? What type? They return to seats and jot three observations in their notebooks — what they saw, where, and what type of waste.

Whole-class discussion: How clean are our school surroundings? Children share their observations. Teacher draws a simple map outline of the school on the board and children point to where waste was spotted. The class discusses: why might waste collect in those spots?
Children write one sentence completing the prompt: 'If the waste I saw is not managed, it could cause ___.' Teacher invites two or three responses to close the unit.

periods.implied_lo: Students can observe and describe the presence and types of waste in their immediate surroundings and connect unmanaged waste to health and environmental harm.
periods.section_context: School surroundings observation, plastic eaten by animals, gases from burning plastic, mosquitoes breeding in wastewater, stagnant water.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask children whether they have seen animals — cows, dogs, birds — near waste heaps in their neighbourhood; this makes the harm concrete and local without requiring an external visit.

periods.textbook_anchor: Ways to Manage Waste — Discuss how clean the school surroundings are and whether waste is found inside or outside classrooms (p. 152)

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens with the question: Do you find waste lying in or outside your classrooms or on the school grounds? Children respond from their fresh observations. Teacher then asks: Have you heard of a neighbourhood, village, or town that people describe as very clean? What made it clean?

Small-group discussion (groups of four): Who is responsible for keeping a place clean — only the person who cleans it, or everyone who uses it? Groups talk, then a speaker from each group shares one idea. Teacher notes the range of views on the board without resolving them too quickly.

Teacher shares the idea from Textbook p. 152 that communities have transformed their surroundings through collective effort. Children discuss: What would it look like if everyone in our class took responsibility for the classroom? What would each person need to do? Class builds a short list of shared actions.
Each child says one thing they personally could start doing. Teacher closes by affirming: when many people do small things, the effect is big — that is what 'shared responsibility' means.

periods.implied_lo: Students can explain that managing waste is a shared civic responsibility and suggest actions individuals can contribute.
periods.section_context: Collective community effort, clean neighbourhoods, classroom and school grounds waste, individual and shared responsibility for cleanliness.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask whether anyone's family participates in a community clean-up, a housing society clean day, or a village sanitation effort; connecting the civic idea to a real local practice grounds the discussion without being prescriptive.

periods.activity_title: Mapping Waste Spots in My Locality
periods.textbook_anchor: Reduce — Draw or paste a picture of a locality, circle waste spots in red, and find out how waste gets there (p. 153)

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces Textbook p. 153 and reads the drawing task aloud. Children close their eyes and picture their street, lane, or neighbourhood: where are the spots where waste collects? They hold that picture in mind before drawing.

Children draw their locality — homes, roads, a park, a shop, whatever is familiar — and use their red crayon to circle every place where they have seen garbage, wastewater, or smoke. Below the drawing they write one or two words explaining how they think the waste reaches each circled spot.

Children share their drawings in pairs, comparing which spots they circled and why. Pairs then share one observation with the class: 'We both circled the corner near the shop because people throw wrappers there after buying food.' Teacher notes patterns across drawings.

Quick whole-class prompt: If you could remove one waste spot from your drawing, which would you choose, and why? Two or three children respond. Teacher affirms that identifying a problem is the start of solving it.

periods.implied_lo: Students can represent their local environment visually and identify specific locations where waste accumulates.
periods.section_context: Locality drawing, garbage spots, wastewater spots, smoke spots, how waste reaches identified locations.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: If children draw different types of localities — a village lane, a city street, a chawl — celebrate the diversity; ask how waste disposal in those different settings might be similar or different.

periods.textbook_anchor: Reduce — Think of ways you can help in reducing waste (p. 153)

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the reduce strategies from Textbook p. 153 aloud: avoiding packaged food, using cloth bags, sharing old toys and books, buying only what is needed. After each, children give a thumbs-up if someone in their family already does this, a thumbs-down if not.

Children open notebooks and write their response to: 'How can I help in reducing waste?' They think of at least three things they can actually do — at home, at school, or when shopping. Teacher circulates and encourages specific, realistic actions rather than general statements.

Children share their lists in groups of four. Groups choose the one action they think would reduce the most waste and explain why. Each group's speaker shares the choice with the class. Teacher builds a class top-three list on the board.

Children read the class top-three aloud together and each privately decides: which of these will I try? No public commitment is required — the choice is personal. Teacher closes by affirming that reducing waste at the source is the most powerful step.

periods.implied_lo: Students can identify and commit to specific personal actions that reduce the amount of waste they create.
periods.section_context: Avoiding packaged food, using cloth bags instead of plastic bags, sharing old toys and books, buying only what is needed.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask whether anyone's family already avoids plastic bags when shopping — how do they carry things instead? This naturally surfaces cloth bags, baskets, and other traditional carrying practices without labelling them.

periods.activity_title: Old Things, New Life — Exploring Reuse
periods.textbook_anchor: Reuse — Explore ways to reuse things: single-sided paper for rough work, refilling steel or copper bottles, making toys or decorative items from old newspapers, calendars, bottles, and boxes (p. 155)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 155 illustrations of reuse examples

time_bands.activity: Teacher asks: Has anyone at home ever turned something old into something new — rather than throwing it away? Children share examples. Teacher then opens Textbook p. 155 and children read or listen to the reuse strategies described there.

Whole-class discussion: The textbook mentions making quilts from old sarees and bags from old cloth. Who in your family does something like this? Children share; teacher affirms these as clever, resourceful practices. The class then lists other reuse ideas on the board — single-sided paper for rough work, refilling steel or copper bottles, toys from old newspapers, decorative items from old boxes.

Children work in pairs and think of one item from home that is usually thrown away. They discuss: what could it become instead? Each pair shares their idea — a cardboard box becomes a shelf, a glass bottle becomes a planter, an old calendar becomes a drawing sheet. Teacher records these on the board.

Children reflect: Why is reusing better than throwing something away and buying something new? Three or four children share their reasoning. Teacher closes by noting that reusing saves both the material and the money needed to replace it.

periods.implied_lo: Students can explain the principle of reuse and give examples of how everyday materials can be used again rather than discarded.
periods.section_context: Quilts from old sarees, bags from old cloth, single-sided paper for rough work, steel and copper bottles, toys from old newspapers, decorative items from old calendars, bottles, boxes.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Prompt children to ask their grandparents or older relatives that evening about one thing they made or repaired instead of throwing away — the variety of traditional reuse practices this surfaces enriches the next discussion naturally.

periods.activity_title: Folding a Paper Bag from Newspaper
periods.textbook_anchor: Reuse — Step-by-step instructions to fold a paper bag using only newspaper, with no scissors or glue (p. 155)
materials: One sheet of newspaper per child

time_bands.activity: Teacher distributes one sheet of newspaper to each child. Together they look at Textbook p. 155 and identify the steps in the folding sequence. Teacher demonstrates the first fold slowly at the front while children watch, holding their own sheet.

Children follow the step-by-step instructions in Textbook p. 155, folding their newspaper sheet one step at a time. Teacher circulates, pausing to help anyone whose fold has gone astray. No scissors or glue are used — the task is completed with folding alone. Children work at their own pace; those who finish early refine the shape or try to make a second bag.

Children hold up their finished bags. They test the bag gently by placing a pencil or small object inside. Teacher asks: Would this bag hold something heavy? What would make it stronger? Children suggest ideas — more folds, thicker paper, bigger sheet.

Quick reflection: Today you turned a piece of newspaper — something usually thrown away — into a bag you can actually use. That is reuse. Children name one other material they could try folding into something useful.

periods.implied_lo: Students can follow sequential instructions to create a functional object from a discarded material using only folding.
periods.section_context: Newspaper sheet, paper bag folding steps, no scissors, no glue, functional bag made from waste paper.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: If a child's fold goes wrong, treat it as a productive moment — ask them to look at Textbook p. 155 again and find which step diverged; this keeps the task inquiry-like rather than demonstration-only.

periods.textbook_anchor: Reuse — Create an item using waste material that you can give as a gift to someone (p. 156)

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the task from Textbook p. 156: create a gift item from waste material for someone you care about. Children spend a moment thinking: Who would they give it to? What does that person like? What waste materials are available on the desk right now?

Children design and make their gift item using only the waste materials on the table — newspapers, old calendar pages, cardboard scraps, cloth or ribbon scraps. They work independently and at their own pace. Teacher circulates and asks individuals about their design choices, encouraging purposeful use of each material.

Children write a brief gift label on a scrap of paper: what the item is and who it is for. They hold up their finished item and take turns in a quick gallery walk — moving around the room to see what others made. No formal presentation is required; children simply observe and admire.

Whole group: What waste material did you use, and what did it become? Three or four children share in one sentence each. Teacher closes by noting that every gift made this way is one fewer piece of waste in the world.

periods.implied_lo: Students can design and construct a purposeful object from waste materials, demonstrating the reuse principle through a creative product.
periods.section_context: Gift item made from waste material, old newspapers, old calendars, bottles, boxes, cloth scraps.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: If children are uncertain what to make, ask them: Is there something small and useful — a bookmark, a holder for pencils, an envelope, a small box — that the person would use every day? Practical utility keeps the reuse purpose clear.

periods.activity_title: Places That Got It Right — Clean Villages and Cities
periods.textbook_anchor: A Place of Pride — Ask elders about villages, towns, or cities known for cleanliness and share findings in class (p. 157)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 157 content on Silluk village, Chhota Narena, Indore, Mysuru

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads aloud from Textbook p. 157 about Silluk village in Arunachal Pradesh — its clean roads, tree-lined paths, national award — and mentions Chhota Narena, Indore, and Mysuru. Children listen and then share: Have you heard of any of these places? Have you visited a place that felt unusually clean? What made it feel that way?

Children recall or imagine: what did people in that clean place do differently? The class discusses what specific habits — not throwing waste on roads, sorting it, cleaning regularly — might explain why a place becomes known for cleanliness. Teacher notes these habits on the board.

Whole-class inquiry: Is there a village, town, or city that people in your family know about for its cleanliness? Children share what they have heard from elders, neighbours, or their own experience. Teacher adds these to the board list. Children discuss: What do all the clean places on the board seem to have in common?
Children each write the name of one place — real or imagined — they would like their own neighbourhood to become like, and one reason why. Teacher invites two or three to share before closing.

periods.implied_lo: Students can describe examples of communities that have achieved cleanliness through collective effort and identify the practices that made them successful.
periods.section_context: Silluk village (Arunachal Pradesh), Chhota Narena, Indore, Mysuru, national award for waste management, zero waste village, Swachh Bharat Mission.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask children whether any elder in their family has visited a place — a pilgrimage town, a hill station, a relative's village — that struck them as exceptionally clean; personal family memory makes the civic examples vivid and immediate.

periods.activity_title: Green Bin and Blue Bin — Sorting Waste
periods.textbook_anchor: Separate Different Types of Waste — Write the names of waste materials that go into each of the two dustbins (p. 159)
materials: Green and blue crayons (one set per pair)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 159 illustration of green and blue dustbins

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens Textbook p. 159 and asks children to look at the two dustbins. What colour is each? Children read or listen to the description of what goes in the green bin (organic waste: dried leaves, fruit peels, vegetable waste, egg shells) and the blue bin (recyclable: metal, glass, plastic, paper). Teacher writes a brief label for each bin on the board.

Children open notebooks and draw two large circles — one green, one blue. Teacher then calls out or writes a list of waste items on the board: banana peel, old newspaper, empty glass bottle, vegetable scraps, aluminium can, plastic wrapper, dried leaves, egg shell, old notebook, broken glass, mango seed. Children write each item in the correct circle, discussing with a partner if unsure. After finishing, pairs compare and resolve any disagreements by reasoning together.

Whole-class check: Teacher points to each item in turn and children call out the bin. For any item where the class is split, teacher invites both sides to explain their reasoning before clarifying. Children correct their notebooks as needed. Teacher then asks: Why does it matter which bin an item goes into? What happens to each bin's contents?
Quick close: Children name one item from home that they have been putting in the wrong place and say which bin it should go into. Teacher affirms that knowing matters only if we actually do it.

periods.implied_lo: Students can classify waste items into organic and recyclable categories and explain why correct separation supports effective waste management.
periods.section_context: Green bin (dried leaves, fruit peels, vegetable waste, egg shells), blue bin (metal, glass, plastic, paper), compost, recycling, colour-coded dustbins.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask whether any child's home or neighbourhood already uses two bins or separate collection — where this exists, that child becomes a resource for the class; where it does not, ask what they currently do instead.

periods.activity_title: Keeping Our Surroundings Clean — Listing, Drawing, and Acting
periods.textbook_anchor: Keeping our Surroundings Clean — List things you can do to keep your home and classroom clean, and draw cleaning tools used in your school or neighbourhood (p. 160)

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads from Textbook p. 160 the idea of taking a pledge on cleanliness and the motto 'Want not, Waste not.' Children discuss: What does 'Want not, Waste not' mean to them? What does a pledge mean, and what makes a pledge different from a plan?

Children open notebooks and write their response to Textbook p. 160: 'List the things you can do to keep your home and classroom clean.' They aim for at least five specific actions — not just 'keep it clean' but 'pick up a wrapper I see on the floor', 'put my lunch scraps in the bin', and so on. Teacher circulates and prompts specificity.

Children make a list of cleaning tools they have seen at home, school, or in their neighbourhood — broom, mop, dustpan, tongs, gloves, dustbin, bucket — and then draw two or three of these tools in their notebooks as described in Textbook p. 160. They label each drawing with its name.

Quick share: Each child holds up their favourite drawing and names the tool. Teacher closes by asking: Of all the tools you drew, which one would make the biggest difference in your school right now, and why?

periods.implied_lo: Students can describe and illustrate specific cleaning actions and tools that maintain a clean home, classroom, and neighbourhood.
periods.section_context: Pledge on cleanliness, 'Want not, Waste not', cleaning actions at home and school, cleaning tools (broom, mop, dustpan, tongs, gloves, dustbin, bucket).
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask children whether cleaning tools differ across homes or regions — a coconut-broom, a phool-jhadu, a mop — to surface regional diversity in cleaning practices without singling any child out.

periods.activity_title: Zero-Waste Birthday Party — Discussion and Poster
periods.textbook_anchor: Keeping our Surroundings Clean — Make a poster to show a village or town managing its waste well, with a suitable title (p. 161)

time_bands.activity: Teacher poses the zero-waste birthday party scenario from Textbook p. 162: imagine you are hosting a birthday party — what waste would be created, and how could you avoid or reduce it? Children discuss in pairs: decorations, food packaging, plates, cups, leftover food. Pairs share their most creative zero-waste idea with the class.

Brief transition: Teacher introduces the poster task from Textbook p. 161. Children think for a moment about what a well-managed village or town would look like — clean roads, sorted bins, people contributing. They choose a title for their poster before they begin drawing.

Children create their poster on drawing paper, showing a community that manages its waste well. The poster includes at least one visible waste-management feature (bins, a clean street, people collecting waste) and carries the title they chose. Teacher circulates with open prompts: What is each person in your picture doing? Where do the bins go?

Quick gallery: Children place their posters on their desks and walk around to see others' work. Each child reads one title from another poster aloud. Teacher closes with the reflection questions from Textbook p. 162: Have you seen waste in nature? What happens to animal waste and dried leaves in a forest? Children respond briefly, connecting the idea that nature manages its own waste — and humans need to manage theirs.

periods.implied_lo: Students can present understanding of community waste management through a creative visual product and connect natural and human waste-management systems.
periods.section_context: Zero-waste birthday party scenario, poster of clean village or town, waste in nature, animal waste and dried leaves in a forest, natural decomposition.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask children to include in their poster one practice that someone in their family or community already does — this roots the ideal town in something real and personally known rather than purely imagined.

assessment_items.question_text: Priya's family finishes a meal and sets aside vegetable peels, bread crusts, and empty glass jars. Priya says: 'The glass jars come from our cooking, just like the peels.' Her brother says: 'No — the peels come from cooking, but the jars came from shopping.' Who is right, and why?

options.label: A
options.text: Both are right; all kitchen waste comes from the same activity.

options.label: B
options.text: Her brother is right; different activities in a day create different types of waste.

options.label: C
options.text: Neither is right; waste is only created when things are thrown on the street.

options.label: D
options.text: Priya is right; all waste comes from cooking activities.

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer: B. The item tests whether students can trace waste to the activity that produced it — a cooking activity creates food scraps, while a shopping activity creates packaging. Accept any reasonable elaboration that names a specific activity for each waste type.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can identify everyday human activities as sources of different types of waste.

competency.competency_text: Describes the basic safety needs and protection (health and hygiene, food, water, shelter, precautions, awareness of emergency situations, abuse, and unsafe situations) of humans, birds, and animals

what_each_option_reveals.D: The child has not distinguished between different daily activities; they treat all domestic waste as coming from a single source (cooking), which is a common over-simplification at this level.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The child holds a street-disposal definition of waste — believing waste only counts when it is littered — and has not connected waste to the activities that produce it.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The child recognises that both children have a point but conflates shopping and cooking into a single 'kitchen' activity, suggesting they have not yet separated activity types from waste types.

assessment_items.question_text: Rajan drew a table in his notebook with two columns: 'Activity' and 'Waste it creates.' He wrote 'Eating an orange' in the activity column. What should he write in the waste column, and how did the orange-eating activity create that waste?
expected_elements: Names at least one specific waste type produced by eating an orange (e.g., orange peel, pip/seed, tissue or napkin used).
Connects the waste to the act of eating — peeling or consuming the fruit leaves behind the unused part.
Shows awareness that the waste did not exist before the activity began.
assessment_items.annotation: Award full credit for a response that names a waste type AND links it causally to the eating activity. A response that only names the waste without explaining how the activity created it is partial. Accept regional fruit names if the logic of the activity-to-waste link is clear.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can record and share observed connections between daily activities and the waste those activities produce.

assessment_items.question_text: There is a large heap of waste near a pond in Meera's neighbourhood. Cows graze nearby and children play close to the pond. Which TWO harms could this unmanaged waste cause?

options.label: A
options.text: Children playing nearby will use the waste as toys, so it is not harmful.

options.label: B
options.text: Cows may eat plastic from the heap and be harmed; mosquitoes may breed in stagnant water near the heap and spread disease.

options.label: C
options.text: Rain will wash the waste away, so there is no lasting harm to people or animals.

options.label: D
options.text: The waste will automatically turn into compost and make the pond water cleaner.

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer: A. Both harms named in A are directly from the textbook's 'Ways to Manage Waste' section. The item assesses whether students can apply knowledge of specific harms to a described scenario.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can observe and describe the presence and types of waste in their immediate surroundings and connect unmanaged waste to health and environmental harm.

competency.competency_text: Describes the basic safety needs and protection (health and hygiene, food, water, shelter, precautions, awareness of emergency situations, abuse, and unsafe situations) of humans, birds, and animals

what_each_option_reveals.D: The child confuses all organic-looking waste with beneficial compost and does not recognise that mixed or plastic-contaminated waste does not decompose cleanly — a misconception that may arise from partial knowledge of the green-bin content later in the chapter.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The child has not engaged with the harm framing; they interpret proximity to waste as neutral or even positive, suggesting the discussion of health risks did not register.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The child holds a 'nature will fix it' belief — assuming rain dispersal ends the problem — and has not connected waste movement to spread of contamination.

assessment_items.question_text: Your class has noticed that the school corridor is often littered with wrappers after lunch. Some children say it is the job of the cleaning staff to pick it up. Others say every student should take responsibility. Write what you think: whose responsibility is it to keep the corridor clean, and what should each person do?
look_for: Recognises that keeping shared spaces clean is a shared responsibility — not only the cleaning staff's job.
Suggests at least one specific action that students can take (e.g., put wrappers in the bin, remind friends, pick up litter they see even if they did not drop it).
Shows understanding that collective small actions together produce a cleaner environment.
Uses reasoning rather than just stating a preference (explains 'because' or gives a consequence).
assessment_items.annotation: A strong response will acknowledge both parties (students and cleaning staff have roles) and argue for shared ownership. A weak response will assign responsibility to one party only without reasoning. Do not penalise children who give a regionally familiar example of community cleaning practice.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can explain that managing waste is a shared civic responsibility and suggest actions individuals can contribute.

Shows understanding that collective small actions together produce a cleaner environment.
Uses reasoning rather than just stating a preference (explains 'because' or gives a consequence).

assessment_items.task: Draw a simple map of your street, lane, or neighbourhood. Use a red circle to mark every place where you have seen garbage, wastewater, or smoke. Below the map, write one sentence for any TWO of the circled spots: explain how the waste got there.
assessment_items.scaffold:
My map shows: [draw your street / lane / area here]
Red circles mark: [name each spot briefly as you draw it]
Spot 1 — The waste got there because: ___
Spot 2 — The waste got there because: ___
format_of_output: A hand-drawn map with at least two red-circled waste spots
Two written sentences explaining how waste reached each circled spot
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any locality the child knows — a village lane, a city street, a school compound. Regional variation in waste spots (open drain, roadside, market area) is expected and correct. Credit any explanation that names a human activity or behaviour as the reason waste is at that spot.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can represent their local environment visually and identify specific locations where waste accumulates.

competency.competency_text: Presents observations and findings through different creative modes (drawing, diagram, poem, play, skit, oral and written expression)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The child can translate environmental observation into a visual representation and articulate a causal explanation for where waste appears.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: Look for whether the red circles correspond to genuine waste-prone spots the child has observed (not random placement), and whether the written explanations name an activity or habit rather than saying 'because people are dirty.'
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: map shows spatial awareness of the locality, red circles are in recognisable spots (corner, market, drain, bin-less area), and the causal sentence names a specific activity (people throw wrappers after buying food, water collects because there is no drain cover). Weak: map is unlabelled or spots are random, and explanations are circular ('waste is there because of waste').
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Children who cannot draw a map may describe their locality in words and mark spots with labels instead of a drawn map; the written causal sentences remain the same.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The task mirrors the textbook activity directly and allows children to demonstrate place-based observation through a creative mode.

assessment_items.task: Think about tomorrow: write a list of THREE things you will do differently to create less waste. For each thing, explain in one sentence WHY that change will reduce waste.
assessment_items.scaffold:
1. I will ___ instead of ___ because ___.
2. I will ___ instead of ___ because ___.
3. I will ___ instead of ___ because ___.
format_of_output: Three written 'I will … instead of … because …' statements
Each statement names a specific swap or behaviour change with a causal reason
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any realistic personal action grounded in the Reduce section — avoiding packaged food, using a cloth bag, sharing rather than buying new, refusing a plastic straw. Regional variation is natural and correct: a child in one region may pack food in a banana leaf, another in a tiffin box. Both are valid. Credit the reasoning sentence as long as it connects the action to less waste being created.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can identify and commit to specific personal actions that reduce the amount of waste they create.

competency.competency_text: Demonstrates how natural resources can be shared, maintained, and conserved (trees, use of rainwater, benefits of millets)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The child can move from the concept of reduction to a personal, actionable plan and provide a causal justification for each change.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: Check that each item names a specific swap (not just 'be less wasteful') and that the 'because' clause explains the waste-reduction mechanism.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: specific, named swap with a clear causal sentence ('I will carry a steel bottle instead of buying a water pouch because the pouch gets thrown away'). Weak: vague generalities ('I will be good') or a reason that restates the action ('I will not use plastic because plastic is bad').
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Children may draw their three swaps instead of writing them; the causal reasoning can be given orally to the teacher if writing is a barrier.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The 'instead of … because …' structure requires children to name an alternative and articulate a reason, directly testing the implied_lo.

assessment_items.question_text: Grandma makes a warm quilt every winter using old sarees that are no longer worn. Neha says this is just because Grandma is old-fashioned. Rohan says it is a smart and resourceful practice. Who has a better reason, and why?

options.label: A
options.text: Both are equally right; it is a personal preference with no environmental meaning.

options.label: B
options.text: Neha, because buying a new quilt is always better quality than one made from old cloth.

options.label: C
options.text: Neha, because modern quilts use new materials that are better for the environment.

options.label: D
options.text: Rohan, because reusing old sarees as quilts means the cloth does not become waste and a new resource is not needed.

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer: B. The item anchors to the textbook's presentation of quilt-making from old sarees as a traditional reuse practice. It tests whether students recognise the environmental value of intergenerational reuse traditions.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can explain the principle of reuse and give examples of how everyday materials can be used again rather than discarded.

competency.competency_text: Describes relationships (including between humans and animals/nature) and traditions (art forms, celebrations, festivals) in the family and community

what_each_option_reveals.B: The child equates newness with quality and has not engaged with the resource-conservation argument; they are applying a consumer-values framework rather than an environmental one.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The child has not grasped that the practice has an environmental dimension; they treat it as a purely aesthetic or cultural preference, suggesting the reuse concept has not connected to the waste-reduction idea.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The child holds a misconception that newly manufactured goods are environmentally superior — the opposite of what the textbook presents — possibly confusing 'modern' with 'better for the environment.'

assessment_items.question_text: Aisha wants to make a bag to carry her vegetables, but she has no money to buy one. She has an old newspaper. Describe TWO steps she would take to turn the newspaper into a usable bag, without using scissors or glue.
expected_elements: Describes at least two sequential folding steps that match the paper-bag making process (e.g., fold the sheet lengthwise, fold up the bottom, tuck or fold the sides to form a base).
Makes clear that no cutting or gluing is involved — the bag is formed by folding alone.
The described steps produce a shape that could hold objects (has a base and open top).
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any two steps that are consistent with a folding sequence — exact terminology is not required. Credit responses that communicate the logic of folding to create structure even if the child uses informal language ('fold it over', 'make it into a pocket'). Full credit requires both steps to be sequentially logical.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can follow sequential instructions to create a functional object from a discarded material using only folding.

competency.competency_text: Uses local materials to create simple objects (family tree, envelopes, origami animals) on their own for display or use in classroom processes

expected_elements: Describes at least two sequential folding steps that match the paper-bag making process (e.g., fold the sheet lengthwise, fold up the bottom, tuck or fold the sides to form a base).
Makes clear that no cutting or gluing is involved — the bag is formed by folding alone.
The described steps produce a shape that could hold objects (has a base and open top).

assessment_items.task: Choose one waste material that is usually thrown away at home or school. Design a gift you could make from it for someone you care about. Draw your design, label the waste material you used, and write one sentence explaining why this gift is an example of reuse.
assessment_items.scaffold:
The waste material I am using: ___
My design (draw it here):
This gift is an example of reuse because: ___
format_of_output: A drawing of the designed gift
A label naming the waste material used
One written sentence explaining why it is an example of reuse
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any waste material and any creative design. The key criterion is whether the child's sentence demonstrates understanding of the reuse principle — not just that they used old material, but that something which would have been thrown away has been given a new, useful life. Regional variation in waste materials is natural and correct.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can design and construct a purposeful object from waste materials, demonstrating the reuse principle through a creative product.

competency.competency_text: Uses local materials to create simple objects (family tree, envelopes, origami animals) on their own for display or use in classroom processes

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The child can apply the reuse principle by designing a purposeful object from a discarded material and articulate why the design exemplifies reuse.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: Check that the labelled waste material is genuinely something that would otherwise be discarded, and that the explanatory sentence names the principle (material is given a new use instead of being thrown away) rather than just describing what the gift looks like.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: design is specific and purposeful, the waste material is clearly identified, and the sentence articulates that the material is saved from being discarded by becoming useful again. Weak: the design is vague or the sentence restates what the gift is rather than why it is an example of reuse.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Children who find drawing difficult may describe their design in words; children who prefer a different mode may construct a physical model using available scrap materials at the desk and describe it orally.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: A drawing shows the design intent and the written sentence checks conceptual understanding of the reuse principle.

assessment_items.question_text: Silluk in Arunachal Pradesh and Indore in Madhya Pradesh are both known for being clean. What do you think the people in these places did together that made them known for cleanliness? Give TWO specific things.
expected_elements: Names at least two collective actions that communities take to become clean — e.g., everyone using dustbins, sorting waste, not littering on roads, regular community clean-ups, managing waste at the source.
Shows that cleanliness is the result of collective effort, not one person or one authority doing it alone.
Connects the named action to the outcome (cleaner surroundings / national recognition).
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any two collective actions that are grounded in the chapter's content. The item does not require children to know external facts about these specific places — it asks them to reason from the principle of collective effort. Credit responses that draw on the child's local knowledge of community clean-up practices.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can describe examples of communities that have achieved cleanliness through collective effort and identify the practices that made them successful.

expected_elements: Names at least two collective actions that communities take to become clean — e.g., everyone using dustbins, sorting waste, not littering on roads, regular community clean-ups, managing waste at the source.
Shows that cleanliness is the result of collective effort, not one person or one authority doing it alone.
Connects the named action to the outcome (cleaner surroundings / national recognition).

assessment_items.question_text: Look at these items: banana peel, old newspaper, empty glass bottle, plastic wrapper, dried leaves, aluminium can. Sort them into two groups — green bin and blue bin. Write each item's name under the correct bin heading.
expected_elements: Green bin: banana peel, dried leaves — both are organic waste that decomposes.
Blue bin: old newspaper, empty glass bottle, plastic wrapper, aluminium can — all are recyclable materials.
No item is placed in both bins or left unclassified.
assessment_items.annotation: Full credit: all six items correctly sorted. Partial credit: four or five items correctly sorted with one or two errors. A common error is placing newspaper in the green bin (paper is organic-seeming); check whether the child is confusing organic material with recyclable material. Do not penalise spelling of item names.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can classify waste items into organic and recyclable categories and explain why correct separation supports effective waste management.

competency.competency_text: Identifies natural and humanmade systems that support their lives (water supply, water cycle, river flow systems, seasons, life cycle of plants and animals, food, household items, transport, communication, electricity in the home)

expected_elements: Green bin: banana peel, dried leaves — both are organic waste that decomposes.
Blue bin: old newspaper, empty glass bottle, plastic wrapper, aluminium can — all are recyclable materials.
No item is placed in both bins or left unclassified.

assessment_items.task: Write a list of FIVE things you can do to keep your home and classroom clean. Then draw and label TWO cleaning tools you have seen at home, school, or in your neighbourhood.
assessment_items.scaffold:
Five things I can do to keep my home and classroom clean:
1. ___
2. ___
3. ___
4. ___
5. ___
Two cleaning tools (draw and label each one):
[Drawing space]
format_of_output: A written list of five specific cleaning actions
Two labelled drawings of cleaning tools
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any region-appropriate cleaning tools — phool-jhadu, coconut broom, mop, tongs, dustpan, bucket. Regional variation in tool names and appearance is expected and correct. The five actions should be specific (not 'be clean') — look for verbs like 'pick up', 'sweep', 'put scraps in the bin', 'wipe the desk'. Credit drawings that are recognisable even if not detailed.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can describe and illustrate specific cleaning actions and tools that maintain a clean home, classroom, and neighbourhood.

competency.competency_text: Presents observations and findings through different creative modes (drawing, diagram, poem, play, skit, oral and written expression)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The child can articulate specific, actionable cleaning behaviours and represent cleaning tools through drawing — combining written and visual expression.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: Check that each of the five items is a distinct, specific action (not a repeat of the same idea in different words) and that the drawings are labelled with the tool's name.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: five distinct, specific actions with action verbs; two drawings that are recognisable and carry accurate labels. Weak: vague actions ('be clean', 'help'), unlabelled drawings, or fewer than the required items.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Children who find listing five distinct actions challenging may use drawings for the action list too, with the teacher transcribing their spoken explanation alongside.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The dual format mirrors the textbook task directly and assesses both written and visual communication as named in the competency.

assessment_items.task: Make a poster showing a village or town that manages its waste well. Your poster must include: a title, at least TWO waste-management features you can see (e.g., colour-coded bins, people collecting waste, clean roads), and a short caption at the bottom explaining what makes this community successful at managing waste.
assessment_items.scaffold:
Title of my poster: ___
[Drawing space for the poster]
Caption — What makes this community good at managing waste: ___
format_of_output: A titled poster drawing with at least two visible waste-management features
A written caption explaining the community's success
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any community setting — village, town, city — and any waste-management feature grounded in the chapter (colour-coded bins, people separating waste, clean roads, community clean-up activity, no litter). The caption is the key conceptual check: it should name what people DO, not just describe what the place looks like. Regional variation in what a clean community looks like is natural and correct.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can present understanding of community waste management through a creative visual product and connect natural and human waste-management systems.

competency.competency_text: Learns about basic social and behavioural norms, values, and dispositions that benefit our social and natural environments and that help our society function smoothly (using dustbins, standing in queues, conserving water, using public transportation, keeping one's environment clean, always helping others in need regardless of background)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The child can synthesise the chapter's waste-management principles into a creative visual argument, showing what a well-managed community looks like and why it works.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: Check the caption specifically: a strong caption names practices (people sort waste, bins are colour-coded, everyone uses dustbins) rather than just describing the appearance (it is clean and pretty). The poster's two features should be identifiable from the drawing, not just assumed.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: titled poster with two clearly drawn waste-management features and a caption that names collective practices as the reason for the community's success. Weak: a drawing of a clean place with no discernible waste-management features, or a caption that only describes appearance.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Children who find extended drawing difficult may make a collage from old newspaper/magazine clippings, or describe their poster design orally with the teacher noting the key elements. The caption can be given orally if writing is a barrier.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The poster format directly mirrors the textbook task and requires children to communicate understanding through a creative visual mode, matching the C-6.2 and C-4.7 competencies simultaneously.
